classification_signals: The paper describes an experiment with participants, a virtual reality setup, and specific experimental conditions (room-size, stroking mode).
It includes dedicated sections for 'MATERIALS AND METHODS', 'PROCEDURE', 'DATA ANALYSIS', 'RESULTS', and 'DISCUSSION'.
Statistical analyses such as repeated-measures ANOVA and Probit analysis are reported with p-values, F-statistics, t-statistics, and beta values.
title: "Seeing" and "feeling” architecture: how bodily self-consciousness alters architectonic experience and affects the perception of interiors

limitations: The study did not directly measure the association between changes in spatial perception and self-location or experienced displacement into the virtual interior, suggesting this for future research.

The lack of stroking-dependent improvement in length estimation for horizontal bars on the front wall might be due to their higher visibility, allowing a more direct comparison with the reference bar.
The interpretation of differences between large and narrow interiors regarding visual scaling of the virtual body is based on previous research and not directly measured in this study.
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated how architectonic interiors modulate bodily self-consciousness using a video-based virtual reality setup. Participants experienced synchronous or asynchronous visuo-tactile stroking while viewing their virtual body in either a large or narrow room. Key findings include that synchronous stroking induced illusory touch and self-identification with the virtual body, independent of room size. In the narrow room, participants reported weak feelings of illusory touch with sidewalls and feelings of approaching walls. Furthermore, length estimation accuracy improved in the narrow room during conditions of illusory self-identification. The study suggests that bodily self-consciousness extends to architectonic elements in close proximity to the physical body, influencing spatial perception. Limitations include the interpretative nature of some findings regarding self-location and the specific task design for length estimation of front wall bars.
